Abstract
Classical proportional–integral–derivative (PID) control is widely employed
in industrial applications; however, achieving higher performance often mo-
tivates the adoption of model predictive control (MPC). Although gradient-
based methods are the standard for real-time optimization, sampling-based
approaches have recently gained attention. In particular, model predictive
path integral (MPPI) control enables gradient-free optimization and accom-
modatesnon-differentiablemodelsandobjectivefunctions. However, directly
samplingcontrolinputsequencesmayyielddiscontinuousinputsandincrease
theoptimizationdimensionalityinproportiontothepredictionhorizon. This
study proposes MPPI–PID control, which applies MPPI to optimize PID
gains at each control step, thereby replacing direct high-dimensional input-
sequence optimization with low-dimensional gain-space optimization. This
formulation enhances sample efficiency and yields smoother inputs via the
PIDstructure. Wealsoprovidetheoreticalinsights,includinganinformation-
theoretic interpretation that unifies MPPI and MPPI–PID, an analysis of the
effect of optimization dimensionality on sample efficiency, and a character-
ization of input continuity induced by the PID structure. The proposed
method is evaluated on the learning-based path following of a mini forklift
using a residual-learning dynamics model that integrates a physical model
with a neural network. System identification is performed with real driving
data. Numerical path-following experiments demonstrate that MPPI–PID

1. Introduction
Inpracticalcontroldevelopment,classicalproportional–integral–derivative
(PID) control remains the established standard. However, to achieve control
performance beyond that of PID control, model predictive control (MPC) [1]
has been actively studied. As computational methods for real-time optimiza-
tion, gradient-based methods are standard, yet sampling-based approaches
have recently attracted attention. Model predictive path integral (MPPI)
control [2], a representative method in the latter category, provides a highly
flexible framework for computing control inputs without gradient calcula-
tions, even when the plant model or objective function is non-differentiable.
This property enables MPPI to handle plant models based on complex non-
linear machine-learning approaches, such as neural networks [3], as well as
control specifications with objective functions involving logical branching [4],
providing substantial practical benefits. Conversely, as MPPI determines
control input based on random samples, the resulting input often exhibits
discontinuities. Furthermore, because MPPI directly optimizes the input se-
quence, it does not retain the standard PID-controller architecture that is
widely adopted in industrial practice, which can complicate deployment and
tuning. In addition, (as with standard MPC) the dimensionality of the opti-
mizationvariablesscaleswiththehorizonlength, whichimposesasubstantial
computational burden.
To realize MPC-based real-time optimization while preserving the struc-
ture and continuity of PID control, approaches have been proposed that
treat PID gains—rather than the control input itself—as optimization vari-
ables and perform gradient-based real-time optimization [5, 6, 7, 8]. Various
2

studies [5, 6, 7] have targeted linear systems, while others [8] have targeted
nonlinear systems based on physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) [3].
However, gradient-based optimization methods are often challenging to em-
ploy when the plant model or objective function is non-differentiable and
require computationally expensive gradient calculations.
Therefore, in this study, we propose a method that updates PID gains—
treated as optimization variables—at each control step via sampling-based,
model-basedoptimizationusingMPPI.Theobjectiveistopreservethestruc-
ture and continuity of PID control while ensuring versatility (for handling
complex control objectives) and computational efficiency. Specifically, the
expected benefits are as follows.
•Handling complex control objectives: As the optimization is based on
MPPI, the method can be applied even when the plant model or ob-
jective function is non-differentiable.
•Continuity of the control input: As the PID control law has a filter
structure based on the integral and derivative of the error, the control
input tends to be smoother than in conventional MPPI, which directly
samples the control input.
•Computationalefficiency: Insampling-basedoptimizationusingMPPI,
computationallyexpensivegradientcalculationsareunnecessary. More-
over, while in conventional MPPI the dimensionality of the optimiza-
tion variables scales with the horizon length, in the proposed method,
thedimensionalityoftheoptimizationvariablesequalsthe(small)num-
ber of PID gains, so improved sample efficiency is expected.
•Compatibility with existing PID controllers: By optimizing only the
PID gains while preserving the PID control-law structure, the method
can enhance performance without redesigning or replacing existing PID
controllers commonly used in industrial applications.
Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights that elucidate the proposed
method. Specifically, we (i) present an information-theoretic interpretation
of an update rule that unifies conventional MPPI with the proposed method,
3

(ii) analyze the influence of the optimization dimension on sample efficiency
through the effective sample size, and (iii) analyze the continuity of the con-
trol input arising from the PID structure.
Among related methods, PI2(policy improvement with path integrals)
[9] is a path-integral-type reinforcement learning approach closely related to
MPPI. PI2, which has also been applied to the tuning of PID gains, is a
model-free method that optimizes control policy parameters on an episode-
by-episode basis [10]. In contrast, the proposed method employs model-
based, receding-horizon optimization at each control step, thereby enabling
online adaptation of the PID gains in response to predicted future tracking
cost under the current operating condition.
Inthisstudy, weapplytheproposedcontrolmethodtoaresidual-learning
model that integrates a physical model and a neural network (Fig. 1). In

Furthermore, we apply the proposed method to system identification and

standard MPPI, demonstrating improvements in path-following performance

4. Discussion
From Table 2, the residual-learning model attains the highest averageR2.
In particular, the velocities(vX, vY)exhibit marked improvement relative to
the physics-based model, indicating that the residual neural network corrects
nonlinear dynamics that are not fully captured by the physics model. The
position(X, Y)and attitude(s, c)already achieve high values at the physics-
model stage, yet the residual-learning model slightly improves them further.
An exception arises in the yaw rater, where the standard neural network
model performs best. As position and speed errors directly influence control
performance in path-following control, the residual-learning model, which
achieved the highest overall accuracy, is adopted for control.
Theproposedmethodsuppressescontrol-inputincrementscomparedwith
conventional MPPI, while preserving tracking performance. This is consis-
tent with the theoretical analysis on the continuity of the control input:
because the optimization variables are limited to the PID gainsθ, and the
control input sequence is computed through the PID structure incorporat-
ing the integral and derivative of the errors, the temporal changes ofa
andδbecome smoother than in conventional MPPI. Moreover, the low-
sample results support the anticipated improvement in sample efficiency.
In conventional MPPI, the dimensionality of the optimization variables is

ing to the number of PID gains. Consequently, the ability of the proposed

5. Conclusions
In this study, we introduce a receding-horizon PID gain optimization
method based on MPPI (MPPI–PID). We establish theoretical insights that
unify conventional MPPI and MPPI–PID within an information-theoretic
framework, and demonstrate, through effective-sample-size and temporal-
correlation analyses, the sample-efficiency and input-smoothness advantages
of the proposed approach. The method is applied to learning-based forklift
path-following control using a residual-learning dynamics model trained on
real-machine data. Numerical results show improved tracking performance
comparedwithfixed-gainPIDcontrolandsmootherinputsthanconventional
MPPI, while retaining favorable performance under substantially reduced
sample counts.
Futureworkincludesexperimentalvalidationonarealmachine, extension
to stochastic control under model uncertainty, and integration with obstacle-
avoidance strategies.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: This partial document introduces "Model Predictive Path Integral PID Control" (MPPI-PID), a novel control method designed to enhance path following performance. The paper highlights the limitations of traditional PID control in achieving high performance and the challenges of standard Model Predictive Control (MPC), particularly its gradient-based optimization and potential for discontinuous inputs. It then presents MPPI as a sampling-based alternative that handles non-differentiable models but can still produce discontinuous inputs and high-dimensional optimization problems. The proposed MPPI-PID control addresses these issues by applying MPPI to optimize PID gains at each control step, thereby reducing the optimization dimensionality and promoting smoother control inputs. The document also mentions theoretical contributions, including an information-theoretic interpretation, an analysis of dimensionality's impact on sample efficiency, and a characterization of input continuity. Finally, it describes an evaluation on a mini forklift using a learning-based dynamics model, demonstrating MPPI-PID's improved tracking performance, comparable results to conventional MPPI with reduced input increments, and superior sample efficiency.

The proposed method aims to combine the benefits of PID control (structure, continuity, industrial compatibility) with the flexibility and performance of MPPI, particularly for non-differentiable models and objective functions. Key advantages highlighted include handling complex control objectives, smoother control inputs, computational efficiency due to avoiding gradient calculations and reducing optimization dimensionality, and compatibility with existing PID controllers. The document also outlines theoretical analyses of the method and its application to a residual-learning model integrating physical models and neural networks, with experimental validation on a mini forklift platform benchmarking against fixed-gain PID and standard MPPI.

The document discusses control methods, specifically focusing on optimizing control inputs for a system. It begins by explaining a residual-based approach where a neural network corrects a physical model, using a mask to select state dimensions and a weighting function to prioritize physical models in data-scarce regions and residuals in data-rich regions.

The document then details two control strategies:
1.  **PID Control**: A classical method that calculates control input based on proportional, integral, and derivative terms of the error from a reference state. It also describes how to handle upper and lower bound constraints on control inputs and their rates of change.
2.  **MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral)**: An optimization method for control problems, especially when the state transition function is non-differentiable. It works by sampling control input sequences, evaluating their performance, and updating the control inputs based on these evaluations. The algorithm involves initialization, perturbation, constraint projection, state and objective value computation, weight calculation, and iterative updates.

A **Proposed Method: MPPI-based optimization of PID gains** is introduced. The document introduces a novel control method called Model Predictive Path Integral PID (MPPI-PID) control, designed to enhance path-following performance for systems like mini forklifts. The core idea is to optimize the gains of a Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller using the Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) framework, rather than directly optimizing high-dimensional control input sequences as in traditional MPPI.

Key points covered include:

*   **Problem Statement:** Traditional PID control is widely used but has performance limitations. Model Predictive Control (MPC) offers higher performance but can be computationally intensive and may produce discontinuous inputs. MPPI is a sampling-based MPC approach that handles non-differentiable models but can also result in discontinuous inputs and high-dimensional optimization.
*   **Proposed Solution (MPPI-PID):** This method applies MPPI to optimize PID gains at each control step. This reduces the optimization dimensionality from the control input sequence to a small set of PID gains, leading to improved sample efficiency and smoother control inputs due to the inherent structure of PID controllers.
*   **Theoretical Insights:** The paper provides theoretical analysis including:
    *   An information-theoretic interpretation unifying MPPI and MPPI-PID.
    *   An analysis of how optimization dimensionality affects sample efficiency, showing that lower dimensionality (like in MPPI-PID) leads to better sample efficiency.
    *   A characterization of input continuity, demonstrating that the PID structure inherently promotes smoother control outputs compared to direct input sequence sampling.
*   **Application and Evaluation:** The proposed method is applied to a learning-based path-following task for a mini forklift. A residual-learning dynamics model, combining a physical model with a neural network, is used. System identification is performed using real driving data.
*   **Experimental Results:** Numerical experiments show that MPPI-PID improves tracking performance over fixed-gain PID and achieves performance comparable to conventional MPPI while significantly reducing input increments. It also demonstrates superior sample efficiency, requiring fewer samples to achieve good performance.
*   **Methodology Details:** The document details the modeling approach (physical, neural network, and residual-learning models), the PID control formulation, the conventional MPPI algorithm, and the proposed MPPI-PID algorithm. *   The residual-learning model is chosen for subsequent path-following control due to its superior overall accuracy.

*   Path-following control is implemented using Model Predictive Control (MPC) based on the identified residual-learning model.
